text: Lesson 1 established that FULL recovery makes a log backup chain possible. This lesson is about actually designing that chain — full, differential, and log backups working together so both the RPO and the restore chain length are things you chose, not things you discover during an incident.

A full backup is the only backup that can restore a database on its own — everything else restores on top of it. How often it runs depends on the database: a small, low-change database can often run a full nightly with no real cost. A large, high-change OLTP database may only be able to afford one a week.

A differential backup captures everything changed since the last full — not since the last differential. Adding a nightly differential turns a worst-case restore chain from a week of log backups into just a few hours of them, because the differential absorbs everything older than last night.

Log backup frequency is really an RPO decision. Backing up the log every 15 minutes means at most 15 minutes of data loss in a disaster. Every choice here trades in the same currency: more frequent backups mean more overhead, but a tighter RPO and a shorter, safer restore chain.

A strategy is correct when it matches the RPO the business actually stated, at a cost the system can absorb — not when it maximizes backup frequency for its own sake. Next up: compressing and encrypting these backups.
